newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori flies to London to salvage Peru's image.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori flies to London to salvage Peru's image.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori left for London on Saturday on a continuing mission to salvage his country's image from a draining hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, which entered its 53rd day.

After an unofficial stopover in New York, Fujimori will take advantage of a Latin American business forum in London to add Prime Minister John Major to the list of world leaders he has tried to impress with his stand against the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding 72 hostages.

He will also try to convince investors they should not dismiss Peru's economic potential because of the siege. "What does Peru lack to be a developed country? We lack nothing," Fujimori said defiantly earlier this week.

But there was little encouragement on Friday for expectations that a solution may be nearer after hopes were raised on Thursday when mediators met MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini in the residence to discuss chances of resuming face-to-face talks with the government.
Police and the rebels resumed their psychological warfare by blasting music at each other, and Cartolini asked his followers through a megaphone: "...What is our objective?"
"To vanquish or to die!" they replied. "Long live the MRTA!"

The government and MRTA have not met since their first face-to-face contact on Dec. 28, 11 days after about 15 heavily-armed MRTA fighters burst in on a cocktail party and seized the residence with hundreds of guests, among them diplomats, government officials and Japanese and Peruvian businessmen.

The MRTA has since freed most of the hostages but has kept its most prized captives, including two government ministers, Japan's and Bolivia's ambassadors, Japanese diplomats and businessmen, and Fujimori's brother Pedro.

Fujimori, who refuses to consider the rebels' main demand for the release of more than 400 jailed comrades, is under pressure to resume talks after promising he would in a meeting with Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Canada last weekend.

Hashimoto said in Tokyo he had "a feeling that (preliminary talks) may get going next week" and mediator Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani said efforts to jump-start talks had "advanced positively" after Thursday's meeting with Cerpa.
"We are starting to unravel things and find a formula to reach the solution we all long for," Peruvian Ombudsman Jorge Santistevan told national television late on Friday.

There was a carnival atmosphere outside the residence on Friday. Mexican mariachis serenaded two Peruvian government officials inside who had their birthdays on Friday and police responded to the rebels' revolutionary hymns with patriotic folk music blasted from huge speakers. Young girls served free lemonade to police and the press and a group of feminists called for a peaceful outcome by decking the road with flowers.
But a four-hour visit to the hostages by a team of medics to check on their heart condition spoke volumes about the unseen hardships and tensions of seven weeks in captivity.
